title: Interactions between chemical species
summary: The forces that hold atoms, ions and molecules together.
cards.0.p: A particle that carries chemical properties is called a chemical species. A chemical species can be an atom (He), an ion (Na+) or a molecule (H₂O). These species attract each other. So how tightly do they hold on?
cards.0.key: A chemical species can be an atom (He, Fe), an ion (Na⁺, Cl⁻) or a molecule (H₂, H₂O).
cards.0.once.soru: What kind of chemical species is Na⁺?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: It is a charged sodium particle that has given up one electron.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: The neutral atom is Na. The + charge shows that the atom has lost an electron.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: A molecule forms when several atoms bond together.
cards.1.p: Attractions that take more than 40 kJ/mol to break are counted as strong (ionic, covalent, metallic), and those that take less are weak (van der Waals, hydrogen bonds).
cards.1.svg#0: Energy needed to break the interaction
cards.1.svg#12: Values in kJ/mol; bars not drawn to scale.
cards.1.svg#13: The 40 kJ/mol line is a convention, not a law of nature.
cards.1.key: This line is not a law of nature but a textbook convention.
cards.1.once.soru: Which one is a strong interaction?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: This bond holds atoms together inside a molecule, and breaking it takes a lot of energy.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: This interaction is between molecules and counts as weak.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: It is a weak attraction between molecules.
cards.2.p: Noble gases have a full outer shell, so they hardly react. Other atoms tend to complete their outer shell to 8 electrons, which is called an octet. H and Li complete it to 2 electrons, which is called a duet.
cards.2.svg#0: Lewis symbol: each dot is one valence e⁻
cards.2.svg#19: Ne has a full octet: it hardly reacts.
cards.2.key: In a Lewis symbol the valence electrons are drawn as dots. The octet is a tendency, and it has exceptions such as BF₃.
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: Neon has 8 electrons in its outer shell. It has no electrons to gain or give up.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: It is the outer-shell electrons that decide reactions.
cards.3.h: Ionic bonds and the ionic lattice
cards.3.p: A metal gives up electrons and becomes a cation, and a nonmetal gains electrons and becomes an anion. Oppositely charged ions attract each other, and this is called an ionic bond. There are no molecules in NaCl. The ions form a lattice.
cards.3.svg#36: Each ion is attracted by its oppositely charged neighbors; there are no molecules.
cards.3.key: An ionic bond forms by electron transfer and the attraction of opposite charges. The formula NaCl only shows the 1 to 1 ratio of the ions.
cards.4.h: Formulas and names of ionic compounds
cards.4.p: In the formula of an ionic compound the charges add up to zero. For example, in Al₂O₃, 2·(+3) + 3·(−2) = 0. A compound is named by saying the cation first and then the anion. NaCl is sodium chloride, and Fe₂O₃ is iron(III) oxide.
cards.4.svg#0: The charges must add up to zero
cards.4.key: Single-atom anions end in -ide. Cl⁻ is chloride, O²⁻ oxide, S²⁻ sulfide, F⁻ fluoride and N³⁻ nitride. For metals whose charge can vary, the charge is written as a Roman numeral.
cards.5.p: In some ions, several atoms carry the charge together. OH⁻ is hydroxide, NO₃⁻ nitrate, SO₄²⁻ sulfate, CO₃²⁻ carbonate and NH₄⁺ ammonium. If more than one of these ions is needed, it goes in parentheses, as in Ca(OH)₂.
cards.5.key: A subscript outside the parentheses multiplies every atom inside them. So Ca(OH)₂ has 2 O and 2 H. PO₄³⁻ is the phosphate ion, and (NH₄)₂SO₄ is ammonium sulfate.
cards.5.once.soru: What is the formula of the compound made of Ca²⁺ and OH⁻ ions?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Two OH⁻ are needed to balance the +2 charge. The polyatomic ion goes in parentheses.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: Without parentheses the 2 multiplies only H, and there are not two O atoms.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: The charges add up to +1, not zero.
cards.6.p: Nonmetals share their electrons, and both nuclei pull on the shared electron pair. This is called a covalent bond. H₂ has one shared pair, O₂ has two and N₂ has three.
cards.6.key: Each line stands for one shared pair. Pairs that are not in a bond are called lone pairs. In H₂O, O has two lone pairs, and in NH₃, N has one.
cards.7.p: In compounds of two nonmetals, the numbers of atoms are given by prefixes: mono, di, tri, tetra, penta and hexa. Mono is not used for the first element. For example, CO is carbon monoxide, and N₂O₅ is dinitrogen pentoxide.
cards.7.key: PCl₃ is phosphorus trichloride. H₂O and NH₃ go by their common names, water and ammonia.
cards.7.once.soru: What is the name of CO₂?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: There is one C (mono is not used) and two O (di). So the name is carbon dioxide.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: Mono is not used for the first element.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: In a compound of two nonmetals, the number of O atoms is given by a prefix.
cards.8.p: The shared pair shifts toward the more electronegative atom. So the H–Cl bond is polar, and the H–H bond is nonpolar. In symmetrical CO₂ the bond dipoles cancel out. Bent H₂O is a polar molecule.
cards.8.key: A polar bond does not mean a polar molecule. The bonds in CO₂ and CH₄ are polar, but the molecules are nonpolar.
cards.9.h: Metallic bonds: a sea of electrons
cards.9.p: Metal atoms let go of their valence electrons, and these electrons move freely through the metal. The attraction between the cations and this sea of electrons is called a metallic bond. That is why metals conduct and can be hammered into shape.
cards.9.svg#12: cations + a sea of free e⁻
cards.9.key: A metallic bond is the attraction between cations and free electrons.
cards.10.p: Weak attractions between molecules are called van der Waals forces. Between polar molecules there are dipole–dipole forces, and every molecule has London forces that come from momentary dipoles.
cards.10.svg#18: a momentary dipole creates a dipole in its neighbor too
cards.10.key: London forces grow as the molecule gets bigger. So at room temperature F₂ and Cl₂ are gases, Br₂ is a liquid and I₂ is a solid.
cards.10.once.soru: At room temperature Cl₂ is a gas and I₂ is a solid. Why do I₂ molecules hold on more tightly?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: In a big molecule the electrons shift more easily. So the London forces get stronger.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: I₂, made of two identical atoms, is nonpolar.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.yazi: There are ionic bonds between them
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: There are only weak attractions between I₂ molecules.
cards.11.p: An ion–dipole attraction happens between an ion and a polar molecule. When salt dissolves in water, Na+ pulls on water's δ− oxygen, and Cl− pulls on its δ+ hydrogens.
cards.11.key: Ions being surrounded by water molecules is called hydration. A polar molecule can create a temporary dipole in a nonpolar molecule, which is called dipole–induced dipole. This is how O₂ dissolves in water, if only a little.
cards.11.once.soru: When salt dissolves in water, which end of the water molecule does the Na⁺ ion attract?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: The oxygen end of water has a partial negative (δ−) charge and attracts the positive ion.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: The hydrogen end of water is δ+ and repels the Na⁺ ion.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: Water is polar, so its ends have different charges.
cards.12.p: The attraction you just saw is formed only by H bonded to F, O or N. H₂O, NH₃ and HF have hydrogen bonds. CH₄ and H₂S do not.
cards.12.key: A hydrogen bond is stronger than van der Waals forces but much weaker than a covalent bond. Hydrogen bonds make ice less dense than water. This is why lakes freeze from the top.
cards.13.p: During boiling, only the attractions between molecules break. In electrolysis, which splits a substance with electricity, the O–H bonds break and H₂ and O₂ form. What decides the type of change is not the strength of the bond but whether a new substance forms.
cards.13.svg#8: the H₂O molecule stays the same
cards.13.key: A strong bond breaking is not enough on its own. For example, melting NaCl is a physical change.
cards.13.etk.soru: Wrap up the topic: match each example with the interaction that holds its particles together.
cards.14.p:
• Chemical species are atoms, ions and molecules.
• Ionic bonds form by electron transfer, covalent bonds by sharing, and metallic bonds in a sea of electrons.
• In an ionic compound the charges add up to zero. Covalent compounds are named with prefixes.
• Van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonds are weak interactions.
• The test for a chemical change is that a new substance forms.
quiz.0.q: Sort each substance by the type of bond that holds its atoms together.
quiz.0.e: In NaCl and KCl, the metal gives up electrons and the nonmetal gains them, forming ionic bonds. In H<sub>2</sub>, HCl and N<sub>2</sub>, nonmetals share electrons, forming covalent bonds. In Cu and Fe, cations sit in a sea of electrons, forming metallic bonds.
quiz.1.q: Match each event with the interaction that explains it.
quiz.1.ciftler.1.0: Oxygen dissolving a little in water
quiz.1.e: When salt dissolves, the ions attract the oppositely charged ends of water, which is an ion–dipole interaction. Polar water creates a temporary dipole in nonpolar O<sub>2</sub>. Water's high boiling point comes from hydrogen bonds. The attraction between nonpolar molecules comes from momentary dipoles (London).
quiz.2.q: Match each formula with its systematic name.
quiz.2.e: In an ionic compound, the cation is read first and then the anion. In FeO iron has a +2 charge, so (II) is written in its name. In N₂O₄, made of two nonmetals, the numbers of atoms are given by prefixes.
quiz.3.q: Which molecule has polar bonds but is itself nonpolar?
quiz.3.e: The C=O bonds are polar, but in linear O=C=O the two bond dipoles point in opposite directions and are equal, so they cancel out.
quiz.3.y.0: H₂O is a bent molecule. Its bond dipoles do not cancel, so the molecule is polar.
quiz.3.y.2: HCl has only one bond, so there is no other bond to cancel its dipole. So the molecule is polar.
quiz.3.y.3: The Cl–Cl bond is between identical atoms, so the bond itself is nonpolar.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Give up an electron, share electrons and set them free.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Sodium has 1 electron in its outer shell, and chlorine has 7. Both tend to complete their outer shell to 8 electrons (an octet).
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: What happens when sodium meets chlorine?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: Chlorine gives one electron to sodium
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: To complete an octet, chlorine would have to give up 7 electrons. Gaining 1 electron is much easier.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Sharing happens between two nonmetals. Sodium is a metal and gives up its electron easily.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: Sodium gives one electron to chlorine
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Sodium gives up its single outer electron and becomes Na⁺ (2-8), and chlorine takes that electron and becomes Cl⁻ (2-8-8). The attraction between oppositely charged ions is called an ionic bond. An ionic bond usually forms between a metal and a nonmetal.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Aluminum forms the Al³⁺ ion, and oxygen forms O²⁻. Add ions until the total charge is zero.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: The formula is Al₂O₃, because 2 · (+3) + 3 · (−2) = 0. As a shortcut, you can cross the charges over. Al's 3 becomes O's subscript, and O's 2 becomes Al's subscript.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: Look for numbers of ions that give a total of +6 and −6.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Increase the number of shared pairs until both nitrogen atoms have a full octet.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.ipucu: Each shared pair counts for both atoms. What should 5 + the number of shared pairs be?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: Three shared pairs formed, making the N≡N triple bond. Each N atom reaches 8 electrons with 3 shared pairs (6 electrons) and 1 lone pair (2 electrons).
A:adimlar.3.metin: The shared electron pair stays closer to the more electronegative atom. First look at the pair between two hydrogens, then replace the second hydrogen with chlorine.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: In the H–Cl bond, where does the shared electron pair sit?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: For the pair to sit in the middle, both atoms must pull equally. That only happens between identical atoms, as in H₂ and Cl₂.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Chlorine's electronegativity (3.2) is greater than hydrogen's (2.2), so it pulls the pair toward itself. Cl becomes partially negative (δ−), and H partially positive (δ+). This is called a polar covalent bond.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Think about which atom pulls the pair harder. Look at the electronegativities.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Metal atoms let go of their valence electrons easily. Connect a battery to the metal.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: The free electrons started to flow toward the positive terminal. This is how a metal conducts electricity. Because the layers of cations can slide, metals can also be hammered into wire and sheets.
A:adimlar.5.metin: An H atom bonded to F, O or N attracts a lone pair on F, O or N in a neighboring molecule. This is called a hydrogen bond. There are hydrogen bonds between H₂O molecules but not between H₂S molecules. We will heat both together.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: Which one boils at a higher temperature?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: London forces are a little stronger in the heavier molecule. But the hydrogen bonds in H₂O are much stronger than that.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: H₂S boils at −60 °C, and lighter H₂O at 100 °C. The hydrogen bonds between molecules make the difference.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The attractions between their molecules are different, so their boiling points must be different too.
A:adimlar.6.metin: The dashed lines show hydrogen bonds between molecules, and the solid lines show the O–H covalent bonds inside a molecule. Now we boil the water.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: Which bonds break when water boils?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: If the O–H bonds broke, new substances such as H₂ and O₂ would form. That happens in electrolysis, and it is a chemical change.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: If the molecules move apart, the attraction between them has been overcome.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: In boiling, only the weak interactions between molecules break. The H₂O molecules stay intact, so this is a physical change.
A:kapanis.0: In an ionic bond, a metal gives up electrons and a nonmetal gains them. Oppositely charged ions attract each other.
A:kapanis.1: In a covalent bond, nonmetals share electrons. Each line stands for one shared pair. H₂ has a single bond, O₂ a double bond and N₂ a triple bond.
A:kapanis.2: If the shared pair shifts toward the more electronegative atom, the bond is polar. Between identical atoms it is nonpolar.
A:kapanis.3: In a metallic bond, cations sit in a sea of free electrons. These electrons carry electric current.
A:kapanis.4: Hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces are weak interactions, and they are what break in boiling. For a change to count as chemical, a new substance must form.
